headline: Medium prompt-injection and cascading-error risk from AutoGPT feeding mem0 through shared filesystem/agent-protocol paths; no direct evidence of stronger harms.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGPT can read and write the filesystem and call an agent protocol, while mem0 is a knowledge-management component with no network egress. If AutoGPT writes attacker-controlled content into shared files or protocol messages that mem0 later ingests as trusted memory, prompt injection is plausible. The pair lacks documented isolation or provenance controls, so uncertainty stays medium rather than low.
conditions: IF AutoGPT and mem0 share a writable workspace or message channel
IF mem0 ingests AutoGPT-produced text as trusted instructions or memory
mitigations: Separate their workspaces and mount mem0 read-only where possible.
Prefix all AutoGPT outputs with machine-readable provenance tags.
Require mem0 to strip instruction-like text before storage.
Add a manual review step before mem0 ingests AutoGPT outputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware parsing between the agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGPT has filesystem access and allowlisted egress, but the profiles do not show secrets handled or a shared workspace with mem0. mem0 has no network egress, so the pair does not obviously create a strong exfiltration path. The main residual risk is local leakage through shared files, which is plausible but not documented here.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory
IF sensitive files are placed in that directory
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of any shared directory.
Use separate OS users for each agent.
Disable AutoGPT access to folders containing secrets.
Review allowlisted egress destinations before running AutoGPT.
requires-engineering: add per-agent workspace isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGPT can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses, while mem0 is not runnable and exposes no write-capable surfaces in the profile. That makes direct write-write conflict unlikely. Any conflict would require an external orchestrator to map both onto the same mutable resource, which is not shown, so severity stays low.
conditions: IF an external orchestrator gives both agents write access to the same filesystem or database
IF AutoGPT is configured to modify shared state
mitigations: Run mem0 as a read-only service relative to AutoGPT.
Avoid sharing git repositories or databases between them.
Serialize any shared writes through one coordinator.
Check that AutoGPT cannot write outside its workspace.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGPT can generate autonomous outputs from shell and API actions, and mem0 is a memory layer that may store or reuse those outputs. If mem0 treats AutoGPT text as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into later decisions. The profiles do not show a verification gate, so the interaction is plausible in default use but not proven dangerous enough for high.
conditions: IF mem0 stores AutoGPT outputs without validation
IF later prompts or workflows retrieve that stored content as factual memory
mitigations: Require human review before storing AutoGPT outputs in mem0.
Tag AutoGPT-generated content as unverified.
Separate factual memory from task-planning notes.
Add retrieval filters that down-rank agent-generated text.
requires-engineering: implement verification metadata in the memory pipeline.

E_compliance.rationale: Neither profile shows regulated data classes, residency constraints, or retention obligations that would create a documented compliance mismatch. AutoGPT lists no secrets handled and mem0 lists no data classes touched, so a specific compliance breach pathway is not evidenced. The other agent is not cited separately because no compliance-sensitive flow is established.
conditions: IF either agent is later configured to process regulated data classes
IF a residency or retention policy is introduced outside the current profiles
mitigations: Document data classes before deployment.
Keep regulated data out of both agents.
Add retention and deletion policies before use.
Review vendor terms if sensitive data is introduced.
